query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the ability to form and maintain a stable, coherent protective oxide layer above 900 °C is primarily governed by the effect of the alloying element X on the metal/oxide interfacial lattice matching and stress accommodation. In particular, when X is Si, its presence facilitates the formation of a dense, coherent Cr-rich oxide (potentially incorporating a silica-like network) that minimizes growth stress and interfacial strain, whereas when X is Mn or Al, the resulting oxide lacks this enhanced coherency, leading to unstable, cracking, or spalling scales.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in either a single-phase or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures exceeding 900 °C.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under controlled high-temperature conditions (>900 °C) in a defined oxidative or corrosive environment (e.g., an O2-rich or SO2-containing atmosphere) while comparing alloy compositions with X = Si to those with X = Mn or Al.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherency at the metal/oxide interface mediated by enhanced lattice matching and reduced interfacial strain. In the Si-containing alloys, the formation of a silica-like phase or network within the Cr-rich oxide scale is proposed to act as a binder that enforces layer coherence.
generation.mechanism: Silicon addition promotes the formation of a protective Cr-rich oxide layer with improved lattice matching to the underlying alloy, thereby reducing growth-induced stresses and preventing defect formation (cracks or spallation). In contrast, the absence of this beneficial effect in Mn- or Al-containing alloys leads to higher interfacial stresses and the development of unstable oxide layers.
generation.predicted_outcome: Si-containing alloys will form a continuous, adherent, and coherent protective oxide layer with minimal cracking or spallation, while alloys with Mn or Al will exhibit less coherent oxide layers that crack or spall under similar conditions.
generation.baseline: The performance of alloys without the beneficial Si addition (i.e., those containing Mn or Al) under the same high-temperature oxidative or corrosive exposure serves as the baseline for comparison.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys in both single-phase and multiphase states when exposed to temperatures above 900 °C under oxidative or corrosive atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative mechanism is proposed based on interfacial lattice matching and stress accommodation, the quantitative extent of the beneficial effect of Si, as well as potential complex interactions in multiphase microstructures, remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy samples with X = Si, Mn, and Al ensuring similar initial microstructures (both single-phase and multiphase as applicable). Expose all samples to a controlled oxidative and/or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C (e.g., 910 °C) for equivalent durations. Characterize the oxide scales using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and adhesion tests to assess scale continuity, thickness, and evidence of cracking or spallation.
measurements: Oxide layer morphology (continuity, thickness, presence of cracks or spallation) via SEM
Phase composition and crystallinity of the oxides using XRD
Mechanical adhesion strength of the oxide scale
Comparative analysis between Si-containing and Mn/Al-containing samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Si-containing alloy does not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in oxide scale continuity, adherence, and reduced spallation compared to the Mn- or Al-containing alloys under identical exposure conditions, then the proposed mechanism—that Si-mediated lattice matching and stress reduction govern oxide stability—is falsified.
